title: BoQ says property slide forcing shift to refinancing
full_text:
Bank of Queensland executives say a sagging real estate market is forcing lenders to offer interest rate discounts to keep customers, given a lack of new loans, with refinancing now the key driver of mortgage volumes.
BoQ reported a full-year cash profit of $325 million, down 15 per cent, after its mortgage book shrank by $4.6 billion over the year to the end of August. But its shares rose 5 per cent on Thursday with the regional lender saying it was on track to restore growth, as its ME Bank subsidiary won over mortgage brokers with sharp pricing and cashback offers.
Overall mortgage demand has plummeted since the federal budget cut property tax concessions for investors, and BoQ said higher inflation and interest rates continued to weigh on sentiment. House prices would probably remain under pressure, further rises in the cash rate were possible, and a reduction was not expected before calendar 2028, it said.
The gloomy conditions are forcing lenders to ramp up customer retention strategies, BoQ chief financial officer Racheal Kellaway told analysts.
"If you look back beyond 12 months ago, we saw high levels of retention discounting in the market," she said.
"It did actually come down through 2026 [but in] the last couple of months, we have started to see that trend back up again. You should expect to see, across the industry, some margin headwinds relating to retention discounting, I expect."
Morgan Stanley analyst Richard Wiles said borrowers refinancing from another bank typically accounted for 35 per cent of mortgage volumes, but this could now represent between 60 per cent and 65 per cent, as new borrowers remain on the sidelines as house prices continue to fall.
"The market we're operating in is more of a refinance market: that is underpinning a large percentage of application volume," BoQ chief executive Rod Finch said.
ME Bank, which BoQ bought five years ago, is one of the few lenders still offering a cashback to entice borrowers. This has helped it win favour among brokers, who provided 72 per cent of new loans over the year.
The cashback is $3000 for loans of $700,000 or more, with at least 20 per cent equity. Mortgage applications of $5.2 billion for three months to the end of August was the highest in a quarter in two years. "We're stepping back in. Service is really key, committing to your time to originate, and you need to be there on price," Finch said. "Cashbacks are a feature in the market these days, and so we will dip in and out of that."
Citi analyst Tom Strong said BoQ had restructured well, reducing costs, but "achieving the full benefits of that work [and] returning to mortgage growth remains subject to a challenging macro environment".
Similarly, UBS analyst John Storey said work to simplify operations and de-risk the balance sheet, including a partnership with Challenger, had led to a stock re-rating, but "going forward, a return to profitable lending growth, notably in mortgages, will be more important". "More efficient capital deployment and further risk transfers should lift [returns], although intensifying competition and tougher industry conditions may constrain this benefit, especially in [this year]," he said.
Finch said he was open to more deals such as the $3.6 billion equipment finance loan sale to Challenger, announced in April. "We learnt a lot through that deal, and it is something that we're open to exploring further, beyond the current arrangement with Challenger."
